transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... I suppose what brings me in is that things have become quite overwhelming lately, and I just needed to speak to someone about what I've been experiencing. You see, I spend a good deal of my time at home in my apartment, and since I'm no longer working, I also try to get out to the museums—I have a degree in the arts, so I've always found museums to be a sanctuary of sorts. But recently, that hasn't been the case at all. What brings me in is that I keep hearing these voices, and they are incredibly clear. 

It started in my apartment, just this... this distinct sound of women whispering. And it's not coming from the hallway or the street outside, it sounds exactly like they are whispering from right behind the walls of my own home. I've even pressed my ear against the plaster trying to understand how they got in there. And it doesn't stop when I leave the house. If I go to a museum and I wander into one of those quiet, empty exhibition rooms where no one else is around, the whispering starts up again from behind the gallery walls. 

And they aren't just making mindless chatter, they are very specific. The women are constantly telling me which photographs belong in the archive. They'll whisper about the displays, murmuring back and forth about which specific pictures need to be archived and preserved, and which ones don't. It's just so constant, this whispering about the photographs, following me from my living room all the way to the empty museum halls, and I just... I don't know how to make them stop organizing the archives.
Do the voices tell you to do anything, or are they just commenting on the photographs?

Well, doctor, it’s... it's not exactly that they shout orders at me like a drill sergeant, but it’s more of a... a profound, undeniable message that I simply cannot ignore. It becomes a compulsion, a very physical necessity to act on what I'm understanding from them. 

For instance, just the other day, there was this museum program I was supposed to attend. It was an educational program, which I always look forward to, given my background in the arts, but when I arrived, I found out it had been postponed. The room was just sitting there, completely empty of people, but full of these metal folding chairs set up in neat little rows for an audience that wasn't coming. And the whispering from the walls, the message I was getting in that moment... it was so overwhelming. I felt absolutely compelled to intervene in that space. 

I started dragging the chairs around—which made this dreadful scraping noise on the floor, I remember that so clearly—but I had to arrange them into a very specific pattern. It was a map, you see. A kind of island map, with different clusters of chairs forming the landmasses and the spaces between them forming the waterways. I spent quite a while getting the geography of it exactly right, dragging chair after chair. And then... well, once the map was built, I couldn't just walk away. Leaving the room would have felt... it would have felt like a deep betrayal, like I was completely disobeying the message I had been given. 

So I went to the very front of the room, at the head of the island map, and I just stood there. I stood there and I lifted my arms straight up into the air, and I just held them there. I had to keep my arms lifted, standing over the islands, because to put them down or to walk out the door would have been defying the entire purpose of what I was meant to do. I don't even know how long I was standing there like that before one of the museum staff finally came in and found me, but I just couldn't leave. So, yes, it’s much more than just commenting on the archives, it’s... it dictates exactly where I need to be and what I must do.
Do you feel like your life is being disrupted or made more difficult by these whispering voices?

Well, doctor, disrupted is... I suppose disrupted is one word for it, though it hardly seems to capture the absolute upheaval of it all. It’s not just a disruption, it’s a complete unraveling of the life I had built. I mean, I used to be so involved, so respected. But now... well, I’ve completely lost the trust of my colleagues. They look at me differently now, with this sort of pity mixed with apprehension, and it breaks my heart because I know I haven't been reliable. I've missed board meetings—important ones, where my input used to be valued—because I was so consumed by the voices and the tasks they set before me. 

And it’s not just the professional side of things, either. The practical matters of living have just slipped through my fingers like sand. I haven't been paying my bills. I’ll sit at the kitchen table with a stack of envelopes, and the whispering from the walls just overtakes everything, and I can't even focus enough to write a check. It got so bad that my cousin had to step in. She’s a dear, really, but having her take over my finances... it’s humiliating at sixty-four to need someone else to manage your money because you simply cannot do it safely on your own. 

Even my appointments, just basic things, I couldn't keep track of them. And then there was the incident at the museum... a museum administrator actually had to intervene. They had to take me aside and handle the situation because I was so lost in what I was compelled to do with those chairs, the map I was building. I couldn't manage myself in a public event, I couldn't be trusted to just attend a program like a normal person. So, yes, the voices, the whispering... they haven't just made my life difficult, they’ve made it impossible for me to function independently. I need all this help now, from my cousin, from the museum staff, just to keep from completely falling apart.
Do you feel any fear, anxiety, or distress when you hear the whispering voices?

Well, doctor, it’s... it’s a complicated question, isn't it? Fear, anxiety, distress... they are such large words, and yet they don't quite seem to capture the exact flavor of what I experience when the women start whispering. It’s not a simple thing to describe, because it’s not as though they are threatening me. They aren't saying they're going to hurt me, or that something terrible is going to happen if I don't listen. It's not that sort of cold, paralyzing terror you read about in thrillers. 

But... is it distressing? I suppose... I suppose I don't really know how to answer that definitively. I don't feel a sudden spike of panic when the murmuring begins behind the plaster. It’s more of a... a profound, inescapable weight. When they start debating about the photographs, which ones belong in the archive and which ones don't, I don't cower in fear. But I am entirely consumed by it. The sheer volume of their presence, the absolute clarity of their voices just on the other side of the wall... it completely overtakes whatever else I might have been trying to think or feel at that moment. 

So, I wouldn't say I feel afraid of them, exactly. I haven't noticed my heart racing or my palms sweating out of terror. But the situation itself, the fact that I cannot escape them, that they follow me from my living room to the empty galleries... well, it’s certainly not a pleasant, relaxing experience. It’s a very heavy, very demanding sort of reality to live in. I just... I don't know if "fear" or "anxiety" are the right labels for it. It's just... it's just my reality now, and it's exhausting, if I'm being perfectly honest.
Have you ever seen, smelled, tasted, or felt anything that wasn't actually there?

Well, doctor, as far as seeing things... or smelling or tasting or feeling things that aren't there... no, I can't say that I have. My senses of sight and smell are perfectly ordinary, really. I don't see apparitions walking around or smell strange odors or anything like you might read about in some peculiar science fiction novel. 

But... well, as I've been trying to explain, what really brings me in to see you, the absolute center of all this upheaval I've been talking about, is what I *hear*. I know we've been discussing them, but you have to understand just how vivid and real it is. It’s those incredibly clear voices in my apartment, and of course, as I mentioned, sometimes in those empty museum rooms when I'm out. It’s not just a vague, muffled sound like a television left on in another room. It’s distinct women, whispering right from behind the walls. 

And they are so intensely focused on telling me exactly which photographs belong in the archive. It's a very specific, very demanding task they are occupied with. I'll just be sitting in my living room, perhaps trying to read or sort through that mail I told you about, and there they are, right behind the plaster, going on and on about the historical merits of these photographs and which ones have to be included. And it’s the sheer clarity of it that’s so astounding. So, no, I don't see them standing in the room with me, and I certainly don't feel them touching me or anything of that sort, but the hearing... the hearing is more than enough. It's why I'm here, really, because listening to these women dictate the archives day in and day out is just... well, it's completely taken over my entire existence.
Have you ever experienced anything like this whispering before in your life?

Well, doctor, if you mean earlier in my life... in my twenties or thirties, or even my fifties? No. Heavens, no. My life was entirely ordinary, quite stable, really, up until recently. This whole... ordeal, it’s a relatively new chapter, though it certainly feels like it’s been going on for an eternity. 

If I really sit down and trace it back, the whispering, and this... this absolute, undeniable certainty that people are watching my archive... it’s all been present for about eight months now. Yes, I'd say right around eight months. I remember because it started as just the faintest murmuring when I was first sorting through some old family albums in the parlor. At first, I thought it was just the wind, or perhaps the neighbors having a muffled conversation. But then it grew into those distinct women's voices, dictating the historical merits of the photographs, just like I told you. 

And right alongside those voices came this heavy, inescapable realization that I was being monitored. That people were watching the archive, keeping tabs on exactly which photographs I was selecting and which ones I was discarding. You can't imagine what it's like to live with that kind of pressure for eight months. Every single day for eight months, waking up and knowing the women are waiting in the walls, and knowing that outside, there are eyes on my work, judging the archive. It completely takes over. I look back at my life nine or ten months ago, before any of this started, and I hardly recognize that woman. So, no, nothing like this before... just these past eight months of absolute upheaval.
Do you really believe that people are watching your archive, or is that just a feeling you have?

Just a feeling? Oh, doctor, no, no, it is certainly not just a fleeting feeling or some sort of... of nervous suspicion. I am absolutely convinced of it. It is a fact. You see, when you are dealing with historical records, with something as monumental as what I am putting together, you upset the established order of things. 

I know for a certainty that the museum board—and not just them, but the city arts people as well, the ones who control the funding and the exhibitions—they have been monitoring my phone. They have to, don't you see? They know exactly what I am doing in my living room. They know that this Caribbean archive I'm compiling is going to completely change how the galleries tell the truth. For decades, they've had their own narrative, their own carefully curated little exhibits that only tell half the story, keeping the real history locked away or entirely ignored. And now here I am, gathering the actual truth, the raw, unvarnished history in these photographs, guided by the women in the walls. 

It terrifies the board. That's exactly why they listen in on my conversations. They need to know who I'm speaking with, what pieces I've selected, how close I am to finalizing the collection. Sometimes I can almost sense them on the line, just waiting to hear if I'm going to reach out to the press or another historian. And honestly, people might try to look at me with pity and suggest I'm just stressed, but no one—absolutely no one—has shown me a single shred of evidence that proves otherwise. Not one person has been able to demonstrate to me that my phone isn't being tapped by the city arts committee. Because they can't. The stakes are simply too high for them to just leave me alone. If this Caribbean archive gets out the way it's supposed to, the entire museum structure will have to answer for it, and they know it. So yes, they are watching, they are listening, and it is far, far more than just a feeling, doctor. It is the absolute reality of my situation.
Do you believe the whispering voices are specifically talking about you or your actions?

Well, doctor, as to whether they are talking about *me* specifically... it's more that they are talking about my *work*, which, in a way, is the same thing, isn't it? Because my actions are entirely consumed by this work. As I was saying—and this is really the whole crux of why I'm sitting here in your office today—I keep hearing these incredibly clear voices. It's mostly in my apartment, especially in the living room where I do the sorting, but occasionally, as I think I mentioned, it happens when I'm out doing research in those empty museum rooms. 

It’s these women, whispering from right behind the walls. And they aren't just gossiping about their own lives or talking about the weather or... or commenting on my clothing. No, they are deeply, intensely focused on my actions regarding the collection. They are telling me, with absolute authority, exactly which photographs belong in the archive. 

So, if I pick up a gelatin silver print from the 1920s, say, a street scene from Havana, the whispering will start up behind the plaster. "That one," they'll say, "that one shows the true architecture before the renovations, it must go in." Or if I hesitate over a portrait, they might murmur, "No, discard that, the framing is a colonial perspective, it doesn't serve the truth." They are narrating and directing my very actions, my choices, my life's work. So yes, they are talking about what I am doing, because what I am doing is the only thing that matters right now. It's just... it's a constant, running commentary on my decisions, day in and day out, guiding my hands as I build this archive.
Do you think anyone else shares your belief that the museum board and city arts people are monitoring your actions and phone calls?

Well, doctor... share my belief? I suppose that depends on what you mean by "share." If you're asking if I have some sort of... of confidant, a partner in all this who sits with me and listens for the click on the phone line, then no. No, I am quite alone in this endeavor. But honestly, how could anyone else possibly understand the magnitude of it? Most people go about their lives completely oblivious to the structures of power that dictate what they see in a museum. They just walk in, look at a painting or a photograph, and accept the little placard on the wall as the absolute, unquestionable truth. 

But I know better. And the board knows that I know better. As I told you, I am utterly convinced—beyond a shadow of a doubt—that the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. They have to be! They know that this Caribbean archive I am building, this collection that the women in the walls are helping me curate, is going to completely dismantle their carefully constructed narratives. It will change, fundamentally and forever, how the galleries tell the truth about our history. 

And you see, when I try to explain this to people... well, my sister, for instance, when she called last month, I tried to warn her. I told her, "Don't say anything sensitive, Beatrice, the arts committee is listening." And she just sighed. She gave me that patronizing little sigh and told me I was overworking myself, that I was letting my imagination run wild because I spend so much time alone with the photographs. But she couldn't prove it! That's the thing, doctor, that is the crux of the entire matter. I told her, "Prove it, Beatrice. Show me the evidence that my line is secure." And she couldn't. No one has. Not my sister, not the superintendent of my building, not anyone. No one has shown me a single shred of evidence, nothing at all, that proves otherwise. Because they can't. The monitoring is real, the threat to their established history is real, and until someone can hand me definitive proof that the city arts people aren't tapping my calls to protect their galleries, I will continue to operate under the absolute certainty that they are. So, no, they may not share my belief, but their ignorance doesn't change the facts of what I'm living through every single day.
Do you believe the whispering voices are sending messages specifically meant for you or about things that are happening in your life?

Well, yes, exactly, doctor. And I know I was just touching on this a moment ago, but honestly, it really is the crux of everything, the... the entire reason I finally agreed to come in and sit in this office today. What brings me in is exactly this phenomenon—I keep hearing these incredibly clear voices, and there is no question in my mind that they are speaking directly, specifically to me. It is not just ambient noise or... or some trick of the acoustics in an old building. 

Whether I'm sitting in my apartment, right there in my living room surrounded by my boxes and folders, or even when I'm out doing research, standing completely alone in those vast, empty museum rooms... I hear them. It's like these women are whispering from right behind the walls, and the messages are entirely meant for my ears alone. They are specifically telling me which photographs belong in the archive, which is, of course, the absolute center of my life right now. 

Why else would they be speaking if not for me? I am the one doing the work! When I'm in the museum, you know, in those closed-off wings where the public isn't allowed, it's so quiet you could hear a pin drop. And then suddenly, clear as a bell, there it is—that distinct, hushed whispering coming right out of the plaster. They know I am the only one who can put this Caribbean collection together the way it needs to be done, so they are sending these instructions directly to me. It isn't some general broadcast for anyone walking by, doctor. It is a very specific, very personal guidance for my project, because this archive is everything that is happening in my life. It consumes my mornings, my afternoons, my evenings... I hardly even stop to make tea anymore because the women are so insistent on getting the curation right. So, yes, to answer your question, the messages are entirely, exclusively for me. No one else could possibly understand what they are asking of me anyway.
Do you think it's possible that your belief about the museum board and city arts people monitoring your actions and phone calls might be mistaken?

Mistaken? Doctor, I... no. No, I really don't see how that could even be a remote possibility. I know people think that, I know they look at me and think, oh, she’s just an older woman sitting alone in her apartment with her boxes of photographs, she must be getting confused. But I am not confused. Not in the slightest. 

If you truly understood the stakes here, the sheer magnitude of what I am putting together, you wouldn't even ask if I was mistaken. I mean, look at it logically. I am entirely, utterly convinced that the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. It’s not a mistake on my part, it’s a calculated precaution on theirs! They know exactly what I am doing. They know that this Caribbean archive I'm building... it isn't just some quaint little historical project. It is a revelation. It is going to completely and utterly change how the galleries tell the truth about our history. The established narratives, the carefully curated lies they've been feeding the public for decades—all of it will crumble when my archive is finished. 

And you ask if I could be mistaken, but... well, as I was saying before about my sister, no one has shown me anything that proves otherwise! If I were mistaken, wouldn't there be some proof? Some simple, undeniable evidence that my phone line is completely secure? I have asked for it. I have waited for someone, anyone, to bring me this supposed proof that I'm just letting my imagination run away with me. But there is nothing. Not a single shred of evidence to contradict what I know is happening. 

Every time I pick up the receiver, every time I hear that faint little click or the hollow echo on the line... it all just points to the exact same undeniable fact. They are terrified of the truth getting out, doctor. Absolutely terrified. And until someone can sit down right here and hand me definitive proof that my calls are private, I have absolutely no choice but to continue my work under the absolute certainty that they are listening to every single word I say. So, no, I am not mistaken. I am just the only one paying attention.
Is there anything that could potentially change your mind about the museum board and city arts people monitoring your actions and phone calls?

Change my mind? Well, doctor, I... I feel like I am just repeating myself at this point, but I suppose if someone were to actually, finally bring me some sort of concrete, irrefutable evidence, I would have to look at it. But honestly, I just don't see how that is even possible in the physical world. 

I mean, really, think about the logistics of the situation! As I have been trying to explain, I am completely convinced that the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. It isn't just a passing thought I had over breakfast; it is the reality of my daily existence. And they are doing it for a very specific reason—they know that my Caribbean archive is going to fundamentally change how the galleries tell the truth. It is going to upend everything they have built! Decades of their carefully curated, sanitized versions of history, just gone, replaced by the actual, undeniable truth that I am piecing together right there in my living room. 

So why on earth would I just change my mind on a whim? People ask me this, my sister implies it, and now you are asking it, but the simple fact remains: no one—and I mean absolutely no one—has shown me anything that proves otherwise! If you or anyone else wants me to change my mind, someone would have to march right into my apartment, take apart my telephone receiver piece by piece, trace every single copper wire all the way down through the walls and out to the street, and show me, beyond any shadow of a doubt, that there is no interference from the city. 

But they haven't done that, have they? Not the superintendent, not the telecom company, not my family. I sit there every single day, meticulously organizing the photographs for the archive, listening to the clicks and the hollow static on the line, just waiting for someone to bring me this magical proof that I'm wrong. But no one has shown me a single thing. Not a shred of evidence. So until that impossible day comes, my mind is completely and firmly made up. The board is listening, the arts committee is terrified, and I will just have to keep working under those conditions.
Have you ever felt like you're in danger because of the voices or the people you believe are monitoring you?

Danger? Oh, no... no, doctor, I wouldn't use the word danger. I mean, not physical danger, not in the sense that someone is going to break down my door in the middle of the night and do me bodily harm. You have to understand the nature of the people we are dealing with here. 

The museum board, the city arts committee... they are bureaucrats. They are people who wear tailored suits and sit in glass conference rooms, terrified of public relations disasters. They use wiretaps and surveillance, they monitor my phone calls, yes, absolutely, but they aren't thugs. They just want to know what I'm doing. They want to know how far along I am with the Caribbean archive because, as I said, they are absolutely terrified of the truth getting out and ruining their established narratives. But they aren't going to physically attack an older woman in her apartment. That's just not how they operate. They want to suppress the work, perhaps discredit me or steal the curation before I can publish it, but danger? No, I don't feel my life is in jeopardy. I just know I have to be incredibly, meticulously careful with my research and who I speak to. 

And as for the voices... the women whispering to me in the museum and through the plaster in my living room... heavens, no, they aren't dangerous at all! Quite the opposite, really. They are my guides. They are the ones helping me piece this entire historical puzzle together. Why on earth would they want to hurt me when I am the only one actually listening to them? I am the vessel for this project, doctor. Without me, their instructions would just be lost to the ether, just echoing around empty museum wings for no one to hear. 

So, no, I don't feel frightened for my personal safety, not in the slightest. I just feel... well, I feel the immense weight of the responsibility, the constant, heavy pressure of being watched by the city, but not danger. I sit with my boxes and my folders, I listen to the women to make sure I get the photographs in the exact right order, and I just keep working. That's all there is to it. No one is coming to hurt me, they are just trying to listen in.
Do you find it difficult to express your thoughts in a logical and coherent manner when the voices are whispering to you?

Difficult? Well... I wouldn't say I find it difficult, doctor, because to me, everything connects perfectly. The logic is entirely sound in my own mind. But... I suppose, yes, when the women are whispering to me, they are giving me so much vital context, so many layers of history all at once, that it can be overwhelming for other people to follow along. 

Take my cousin, for example. She will come over or call me, and she’ll ask a completely mundane, simple question. Something about a utility bill, or maybe reminding me about an appointment. Just a tiny, isolated little detail of daily life. But nothing is isolated! The women are whispering about the connections, so to give her a proper answer, I have to start by explaining the grant. Because the grant is what funds the preservation, you see? And you simply cannot understand the grant without understanding the historical context of the Caribbean shipping routes. I mean, the routes dictated exactly how the artifacts and the photographs traveled between the islands and the mainland. So I'll be explaining the shipping manifests, and that naturally leads me directly to my grandmother’s altar, because the items on that altar—the brass bells, the lace, the specific way the candles were arranged—they all came along those exact same routes! 

It’s a beautiful, intricate web of history, and I try to explain it all to her so she understands the full picture. But... well, I will go on like this, laying out all these undeniable connections, and by the time I finally stop talking and take a breath, she is just staring at me. Nobody seems to know what I meant. My cousin will just look completely lost, as if we aren't even speaking the same language. She just wanted to know about a piece of mail, and I've given her the entire history of the diaspora. So, yes, I suppose my thoughts come out in a way that other people find difficult to follow, but it's only because they aren't hearing the full story the way the voices are explaining it to me.
Do you think the museum board and city arts people would stop monitoring you if you stopped working on the Caribbean archive?

Stop working on the archive? Oh, doctor, I... I don't think you fully grasp the magnitude of what we are dealing with here. If I were to just stop—which I would never do, mind you, because the women would be so disappointed and the history would just be lost—but if I did, hypothetically, just pack up the boxes and put the folders away... no, I don't think they would stop. Not for a second. 

You see, it isn't just about the work I am doing today or tomorrow. It is about what I already know! I am completely convinced that the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone for months now, and they know what I have already uncovered. They know that I have seen the connections between the old shipping manifests and the sanitized plaques they put up in the galleries. My Caribbean archive is going to completely change how the galleries tell the truth. It will dismantle their entire narrative! And once you know something like that, once you hold that truth in your hands, you can't just un-know it. They know I have the knowledge. 

So, if I stopped working, they would just assume I was hiding it. They would probably monitor me even more closely! They would think, 'Oh, she's gone quiet, she must be preparing to release it to the press,' or 'She's secretly handing it off to an independent curator.' They would never believe I just stopped. And frankly, why should I believe they would stop listening? As I said before, no one has shown me anything that proves otherwise! Not a single person has brought me a shred of evidence to show that my phone isn't tapped or that the arts committee isn't keeping tabs on me. Until someone can physically prove to me that the line is clear—which they haven't—I have to assume they are always there, always listening, whether I am actively sorting photographs or just sitting in my armchair drinking tea. The truth is already out there in my living room, doctor, and they are terrified of it.
Do you think it's possible that the museum board and city arts people are not actually monitoring your actions and phone calls, and that this belief is something that only you think is happening?

Possible? Well... I mean, people do say that to me, doctor. They say, oh, maybe it’s just your imagination running away with you, maybe you’re just working too hard on the research. But no. No, I don't think it's just me, and I certainly don't think it's just some... some fantasy I've cooked up in my head. 

I am absolutely, one hundred percent convinced that the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. It isn't a guess. You just have to look at the motives, really. It’s simple cause and effect. They know exactly what I am doing because they know my Caribbean archive will completely change how the galleries tell the truth. For decades—longer, really, if you look at the entire institutional history of this city—they have relied on these very neat, very sanitized little plaques to explain away the diaspora and the trade routes. And here I am, sitting in my living room, compiling the actual, undeniable truth that is going to dismantle all of that. I am going to force them to change the galleries. Why wouldn't they monitor me? Frankly, from a bureaucratic standpoint, it would be foolish of them not to keep tabs on me! They have the budget for it, I've seen the public arts funding allocations, and with digital networks today, they don't even need to park a van outside, they just route the surveillance right through the city servers. 

And as for the idea that it's only happening in my mind... well, if that were true, why hasn't a single person been able to prove me wrong? No one has shown me anything that proves otherwise. Not my cousin, not the telephone company, not you. People are so quick to tell me I’m mistaken, but nobody has actually come to my apartment, taken apart my phone, and shown me that the line is clear. Nobody has brought me a shred of tangible, physical evidence to show that the arts committee isn't listening in. I am a researcher, doctor. I have a degree, I respect evidence, and I look at the facts. But there is no evidence to the contrary! None whatsoever. They just expect me to blindly trust that I have privacy, while the most important historical work of the decade is sitting in boxes on my coffee table. 

So, until someone can actually hand me proof—real proof—that the board isn't listening to every single call I make, I have to operate under the absolute certainty that they are. Because they are terrified of the archive, doctor. They are terrified of the truth. And I won't let anyone tell me I'm just imagining things when the stakes for the history of those galleries are this high.
Is there anything that could make you question or doubt the voices and the monitoring you believe is happening?

Question it? Doubt it? Well, doctor... I suppose if you want to speak purely in hypotheticals, yes, a person could doubt something if they were presented with overwhelming, irrefutable evidence to the contrary. I am a rational woman, after all. I have my degree. I spent years in university learning how to evaluate historical documents, how to weigh primary sources against secondary accounts, how to build a proper thesis. So, theoretically, if someone—say, an independent telecommunications expert, and certainly not someone on the city payroll, mind you—if they came into my apartment, physically dismantled my telephone, ran a complete diagnostic sweep of the wiring all the way down to the street level, and handed me a certified, signed report saying there were no intercepts... well, then, I might pause. I might sit down with a cup of tea and say, 'Alright, let us re-evaluate the situation.' 

But do you see the problem here, doctor? That hasn't happened! Not once! People just sit in chairs across from me and ask if I have doubts, but they don't do the work. They don't bring me the proof! So how can I possibly question it? I am absolutely, unequivocally convinced that the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. I know it in my bones. And it makes perfect, logical sense because they know exactly what I hold in those boxes on my coffee table. They know my Caribbean archive will fundamentally change how the galleries tell the truth about our history. It will completely rewrite the sanitized little plaques on their walls! 

So, no, I don't doubt it for a single second, because no one has shown me anything—not a single, solitary piece of tangible evidence—that proves otherwise. They just want me to doubt myself so I'll stop working. They want me to second-guess the women whispering to me, to second-guess the historical connections I'm making, because it would be so much more convenient for them if I just went quietly mad.
